ety.text: From Middle English murder, murdre, mourdre, alteration of earlier murthre (“murder”) (see murther), from Old English morþor (“secret slaying, unlawful killing”) and Old English myrþra (“murder, homicide”), both from Proto-West Germanic *morþr, from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“death, killing, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥tro- (“killing”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *mor-, *mr̥- (“to die”). Akin to Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌸𐍂 (maurþr, “murder”), Old High German mord (“murder”), Old Norse morð (“murder”), Old English myrþrian (“to murder”) and morþ.

senses.d: An act of killing a person unlawfully, especially with predetermination.
ex: Throwing that punch was a murder whether you meant for it to happen or not.
There have been ten unsolved murders this year alone.

senses.d: The crime of killing a person unlawfully, especially with predetermination.
ex: The defendant was charged with murder.

senses.d: The act of killing any being in an immoral manner; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: Meat is murder.

senses.d: Synonym of murderer , a person who has unlawfully killed another.
Something difficult or terrible to endure.
ex: I heard this class is murder.
This headache is murder.
Right quick another cat spoke up real loud, saying, “That’s murder man, really murder,” and his eyes were signifying too.

senses.d: A flock of crows or sometimes ravens.
ex: A murder of crows dotted my backyard.
Every morning we woke up to the squawking of what seemed like a hundred murders in the trees above our campsite.

senses.d: To illegally kill (a person or persons) with intent, especially with predetermination
ex: The woman found dead in her kitchen was murdered by her husband.
My uncle’s dog murdered my cat.
Our team is going to murder them.

senses.d: To kick someone's ass or chew someone out (used to express one’s anger at somebody).
ex: He's torn my best shirt. When I see him, I'll murder him!
I could murder a hamburger right now.
“Is that so? Well, I could murder a cup of tea,” said Auntie Flip.
